Eﬀect of Propane Addition and Oxygen Enrichment on the Flame
Characteristics of Biogas
Xi Wang, Ligang Zheng,* Jian Wang, Rongkun Pan, Wen Yang, Hongwang Jin, and Yuanpeng Fu
Cite This: Energy Fuels 2021, 35, 5015−5025
Read Online
ACCESS

*

ABSTRACT: Mixing biogas with other fuels or increasing the oxygen
fraction in the oxidizer can improve the combustion performance of
biogas. In this study, we investigated the eﬀects of propane addition and
oxygen enrichment on the ﬂame characteristics of biogas with a constant
heating value in a half-open duct. The evolution of the ﬂame structure
revealed that the tulip structure took on two types of patterns at the
oxygen fraction θ = 0.21. However, there was no salient tulip ﬂame
formation when θ > 0.21. Oxygen enrichment signiﬁcantly increased the
ﬂame propagation velocity (V) and explosion pressure (P). Propane
addition signiﬁcantly reduced Vmax at θ = 0.25 and 0.29. The maximum
rate of pressure rise [(dP/dt)max] exhibited a nonlinear dependence on
the maximum ﬂame velocity (Vmax). A similar trend was observed for
the dependence of (dP/dt)max on the laminar burning velocity (LBV). Therefore, the LBV is an important parameter to predict Vmax
and (dP/dt)max values of mixtures. Furthermore, by using the PREMIX code and the UC San Diego mechanism, we simulated
laminar ﬂame burning properties to reveal the macroscopic ﬂame propagation characteristics. The rate of propane consumption was
higher than the rate of methane consumption. Additionally, oxygen enrichment played an important role in the entire reaction
process, leading to an increase in the molar concentrations of microscopic free radicals and a promotion of the rates of production
(ROP) of free radicals. In contrast, the addition of propane decreased the molar concentrations of microscopic free radicals and
inhibited the ROP of free radicals.
1. INTRODUCTION
Currently, more than 85% of the world’s energy demands is
met by fossil fuels.1 The emission of CO2 and NOx is
increasing continuously, which has led to a signiﬁcant
greenhouse eﬀect and air pollution.2 Growing concerns
regarding the amount of these gases emitted into the
environment and predictions of the exhaustion of petroleum-
derived fuels have motivated the development of clean energy.3
Biogas is produced through bacterial conversion of organic
matter under anaerobic conditions and is a mixture of CH4 and
CO2, with small amount of H2S, N2, CO, and O2.3,4 Compared
with traditional fossil fuels, biogas has the advantages of
abundant availability and lower pollution.3 It is also very
appropriate for power generation, heating systems, and other
applications.4 Interest in the use of biogas as an increasingly
renewable and sustainable energy source has been promoted
recently.5 Dupont and Accorsi6 investigated biogas explosion
characteristics at various temperatures (30−70 °C) and at
atmospheric pressure. Anggono et al.7 determined the
ﬂammability limits of biogas−air mixtures using spherically
expanding ﬂames propagating. Ratna Kishore et al.8 studied the
adiabatic burning velocities for natural-gas-like mixtures over a
range of equivalence ratios at atmospheric pressure. Hinton
and Stone9 measured the laminar burning velocity (LBV) of
biogas over a wide range of temperatures and pressures. Zeng
et al.10 investigated the main factors inﬂuencing the
combustion stability and LBV of biogas in laminar burning
inside a constant-volume combustion chamber using a
schlieren system.
However, biogas has an extremely low energy density, low
propagation velocity, and narrower ﬂammability ranges based
on large amounts of inert gas (i.e., CO2).11 These character-
istics have hindered the popularization of biogas. On the basis
of these shortcomings, two methods have been developed to
improve the combustion performance of biogas: mixing biogas
with other fuels with superior characteristics or increasing the
oxygen fraction in the oxidizer.12 To evaluate both methods,
this study raises the possibility of investigating the eﬀect of
propane addition and oxygen enrichment on the explosion
characteristics of biogas.
A well-established alternative to gasoline is liqueﬁed
petroleum gas, where propane is a major component.13−15

The lower heating value of propane is 83.470 MJ/m3, which is
2.33 times that of methane (35.823 MJ/m3).16 Propane has
been mixed with biogas to improve its combustion properties
in previous studies.17−19 Law20 and Kwon demonstrated that
propane addition reduces the knocking occurrence of an
internal combustion engine. Schuh et al.21 demonstrated that
propane addition reduces the ignition delay time of the
methane−propane blends. Gómez Montoya et al.22 pointed
out that biogas mixtures with propane yield increased output
power and generation eﬃciency for spark ignition biogas
engines. Lee et al.23 determined the burning velocities of
biogas and biogas/propane mixtures. Luo et al.24 measured the
upper and lower ﬂammability limits and explosive risk values
for diﬀerent mixtures of CH4 and C3H8. Petersen et al.18
investigated the ignition and oxidation kinetics of CH4−C3H8
mixtures at gas turbine pressures by shock tube experiments
and chemical kinetic modeling. Cardona and Amell12
determined that biogas/propane/hydrogen mixtures have
higher a LBV than pure biogas at 0.828 atm and 298 K
while varying the air/fuel ratio.
Oxygen-rich combustion technology25,26 can improve the
combustion eﬃciency of biogas12,22,27 and reduce CO2 and
NOx emissions.1,28,29 The concept of mixing these fuels is not
new. However, compared to the study of a single fuel such as
biogas and propane, there are relatively few published studies
reporting the inﬂuence of propane addition and oxygen
enrichment on the explosion characteristics of biogas. The
increasing applications of biogas will introduce additional
safety issues.25,30,31 In addition, the typical phenomenon of
combustion-induced rapid phase transition (CRPT) of a
closed-vessel explosion can induce anomalous impulses in the
pressure history in oxygen-enriched air.25,31 Benedetto et
al.32,33 indicated that the CRPT can be mitigated by the
presence of CO2.
In real workplaces, biogas can be leaked into a conﬁned
space of large length-to-diameter ratios, such as tunnels,
passageways, pipelines, silos, and mines, forming an explosion
of any concentration of fuel−air mixtures within the explosion
limits.4,30 There is little knowledge about the ﬂame
propagation and pressure dynamics of biogas explosions in
conﬁned spaces that have a similar geometry of large length-to-
width ratios. Furthermore, compared with freely propagating
ﬂames, the premixed ﬂame will behave in a much more
complicated manner when the ﬂame propagates in a duct of
large length-to-width ratio. In a suﬃciently long, smooth duct,
the laminar ﬂame will undergo a series of structural changes.
The most interesting and attractive ﬂame shape is a tulip
ﬂame.34−36 Furthermore, with propane addition and oxygen
enrichment of biogas, complex fuel compositions can lead to
unpredictable combustion performance.
Overall, this work aimed to study the eﬀects of propane
addition and oxygen enrichment on the ﬂame characteristics of
biogas experimentally in a half-open rectangular duct over a
wide range of mixture compositions while the heating value of
the blended fuel remained constant. This study provides
experimental data and theoretical guidance for the combustion
of biogas containing C3H8 and O2 in a half-open duct. It is
important to determine the ﬂame acceleration mechanisms
behind the deﬂagration-to-detonation transition, which are
relevant for safety in transport pipelines, silos, and mines.
2. EXPERIMRNTAL SETUP
A schematic diagram of the experimental system is shown in Figure 1,
similar to those of the previous studies.37,38 All experiments were
conducted in a transparent plexiglass explosion duct with a cross-
sectional area of 100 × 100 mm2, length of 1000 mm, and volume of
10 L, which can withstand the pressure of 2 MPa. The left end of the
duct was sealed with a PVC ﬁlm as a relief vent, and the opposite end
was sealed with rubber pads and TP304 steel plates. A pair of spark
electrodes was centrally ﬂush with the steel plate at the right end of
the duct, and the ignition voltage was 6 V. The transient ﬂame
development process was recorded by a high-speed camera (Dantec
Corp.). Two pressure transducers (Shanghai MingKong Sensor
Technology Ltd.) were employed to collect the dynamic pressure
details in the duct. One pressure transducer installed at the bottom
sidewall was 10 cm away from the open end, and another was installed
on the steel plate at the right end of the duct. The acquisition
frequency of the data acquisition card (model USB-1608Plus) was 15
kHz. In addition, a synchronization controller was used to ensure
synchronous operation of the pressure transducers, the high-speed
camera, and the ignitor, which facilitates coupling the analysis of ﬂame
development and pressure history.
The mixture consisted of CH4, C3H8, O2, CO2, and dry air. The
purity of CH4, C3H8, O2, and CO2 were 99.995%, 99.99%, 99.995%,
and 99.99%, respectively. The air is compressed air, and the ratio of
the nitrogen to oxygen volume is 79:21. All the gases except air were
produced by Jining Xieli Special Gas Co., Ltd. Five mass ﬂow

3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSSION
3.1. Flame Structure Characteristics. Figure 2 presents
the evolution of the ﬂame structure over time for each
combination of oxygen fraction θ and propane fraction μ.
When the oxygen fractions θ are 0.35, 0.40, and 0.50, the ﬂame
structural evolution is similar to that for θ = 0.29. Therefore,
they are not represented in Figure 2.
As shown in Figure 2a, when the oxygen fraction is θ = 0.21,
a typical tulip ﬂame appears; i.e., the ﬂame convex toward the
unburned gas changes to one convex toward the burned
gas.35,39 In the case of μ = 0.43 in Figure 2a, a salient tulip
ﬂame can be observed. The ﬂame gradually evolves from a
hemisphere (t = 20 ms) to a ﬁnger shape (t = 40 ms), a ﬂat
shape (t = 75 ms), and a tulip ﬂame (t = 95 ms). As θ increases
to 0.25, the reactivity of the mixture is enhanced. The tulip
ﬂame became distorted and the ﬂame surface became
progressively wrinkled. As θ increases from 0.25 to 0.29, only
hemispherical and ﬁnger ﬂames form, the ﬂame front becomes
more slender, and the luminance of the ﬂame increases. The
ﬂames quickly pass out of the duct without forming a tulip
ﬂame, as shown in Figure 2c.
Zheng et al.38 found that depending on oxygen fraction and
equivalence ratio, the tulip structure of CH4/O2/CO2 mixtures
takes on three types of patterns. Alabaş et al.40 indicated that
compared to the combustion of pure methane with air,
increasing the oxygen enrichment to 24% increases the
combustion stability, but the stability decreases again at 26%
oxygen enrichment under acoustic enforcement. What is more,
oxygen enrichment has a signiﬁcant inﬂuence on ﬂame
structure evolution in Figure 2. In addition, for θ = 0.21,
when increasing the propane fraction μ from 0.00 to 0.43,
there are diﬀerent evolutionary processes for the tulip ﬂame.
Speciﬁcally, the evolution times of the diﬀerent ﬂame stages are
extended. However, for θ > 0.21, there are no obvious changes
in the ﬂame structure as μ increases.
For θ = 0.21, the tulip structure takes on two types of
patterns with varying propane fraction. The ﬁrst type is
presented in Figure 3a, where one can see a classic tulip ﬂame
at 76 ms. Subsequently, the two tongues of the ﬂame front
continue to convex toward the unburned gas. It is obvious that
the upper tongue travels faster than the lower tongue (see the
ﬂame images at 88, 89, and 92 ms) in Figure 3a. The position
of the cusp that sags into the burned gas remains stationary
relative to the closed end of the duct, as indicated by the red
line in Figure 3a. Therefore, the more slender upper tongue
protrudes forward as if the ﬂame is ﬂoating above. This
asymmetric ﬂame propagation pattern could be attributed to
buoyancy.2,9,10 Hinton and Stone9 demonstrated that the
buoyancy has a signiﬁcant impact on the ﬂame propagation
when the LBV is less than 15 cm/s. As shown in Figure 4, all of
the LBVs were greater than 30 cm/s in this study. Therefore,
buoyancy is not the origin of the asymmetric ﬂame tongues. In
this set of experiment, the PVC ﬁlm ﬁrst ruptured in the upper
section, resulting in a stronger gas ﬂow in the upper section
than in the lower section, which has a greater impact on the
upper tongue. The second type of tulip ﬂame formation is
presented for μ = 0.43 in Figure 3b. The ﬂame structure
develops into a classic tulip at 97 ms, and then the upper and
lower tongues of the ﬂame front elongate toward the unburned
gas in a symmetric manner. Compared to the cusp position at
θ = 0.21 and μ = 0.00, the cusp position at θ = 0.21 and μ =
0.19 moves forward (see the ﬂame images at t = 97, 110, and
117 ms that are marked by red lines). Additionally, the upper
and lower tongues become thicker, move toward the duct axis,
and then gradually merge into each other.
The ﬂat ﬂame is the signature of the formation of the tulip
ﬂame (the transition of the ﬂame curvature from positive to
negative signiﬁes the occurrence of the tulip ﬂame). As shown
in Figure 2, the ﬂat ﬂame can only be observed at θ = 0.21 and
0.25. As the propane fraction μ increases, the formation
distance of the ﬂat ﬂame gradually decreases (the ignition end
is the zero point on the coordinate axis), as shown in Figure 5.
As θ increases from 0.21 to 0.25, the formation distance of the
ﬂat ﬂame clearly increases. Additionally, there is a consistent
increase in the formation time of a ﬂat ﬂame when μ increases
(from 61 to 75 ms for θ = 0.21 and from 31 to 46 ms for θ =
0.25). Di Benedetto et al.12,45,46 demonstrated that oxygen
enrichment increases the reactivity of a mixture, thereby
increasing the LBV. The LBV increases with increasing θ, but it
decreases with an increase in μ, as shown in Figure 4. For a
ﬁxed duct length, higher reactivity results in a shorter ﬂame
residence time and a longer ﬂat ﬂame formation distance.

3.2. Flame Tip Dynamics. Figure 6 presents the ﬂame
front velocity (V) with various propane fractions μ and oxygen
fractions θ. All data come from the same runs as the images of
Figure 2. Prior to ﬂame inversion, the ﬂame tip propagating
along the duct axis is called the ﬂame front. After the ﬂame
inversion, the ﬂame tip near the upper and lower side walls is
called the ﬂame front. Ztip is deﬁned as the distance between
the ﬂame tip to the ignition position, and V is the time
derivative of Ztip.
As shown in Figure 6, the ﬂame front velocity proﬁles are
divided into three patterns. In the ﬁrst pattern, following initial
acceleration, the ﬂame front decelerates sharply and the
velocity drops to the minimum. The acceleration process is
then repeated again, which can be clearly observed at θ = 0.21.
In the second pattern, there is no second acceleration after the
ﬂame exhibits acceleration and deceleration, but the deceler-

When the ﬂame structure develops into hemispherical and
ﬁnger shapes, the ﬂame is in a laminar burning regime. In this
regime, the ﬂame surface area increases exponentially,34,35
which increases the ﬂame propagation and forms the initial
ﬂame acceleration. The ﬁrst deceleration is caused by the ﬂame
being partially extinguished by contact with the sidewalls.34
The ﬂame surface curvature becomes smaller and the ﬂame
surface area decreases. Subsequently, the ﬂame front structure
reverses and gradually forms a tulip ﬂame, and then the ﬂame
front gradually curls and wrinkles, increasing the ﬂame surface
area. Next, the reaction intensity and heat release rate increase
continuously, leading to the second acceleration. No salient
tulip ﬂame can be observed for θ = 0.25. Therefore, the second
acceleration is not presented in Figure 6b. As the oxygen
fraction increases, the mixture reactivity continues to increase,
and the explosion becomes more violent. The quenching eﬀect
of the sidewall cannot counteract the ﬂame propagation
enhancement caused by this intense combustion, resulting in a
continuous increase in ﬂame velocity, as shown in Figure 6c.
Figure 7 presents the propagation time of the ﬂame from
ignition to exiting the duct. The red brackets indicate that, as θ
increases from 0.21 to 0.25, 0.29, 0.35, 0.40, and 0.50, the
decrease in the ﬂame propagation time between adjacent
oxygen fractions is 63.1%, 35.3%, 31.8%, 30.1%, and 23.8%,
respectively. The diﬀerence between 63.1% and 23.8% is
signiﬁcant. Additionally, the black arrows indicate that as μ
increases from 0.00 to 0.16, 0.19, 0.23, 0.26, 0.28, 0.31, and
0.43, the decreases in ﬂame propagation time are 21.4%,
32.1%, 31.3%, 25.2%, 36.4%, and 27.3% for the six oxygen
fractions, respectively. The diﬀerence between 36.4% and
21.4% is relatively small. Compared to propane addition,
oxygen enrichment is more eﬀective at reducing the ﬂame
propagation time. It is noteworthy that as θ increases from 0.21
to 0.25, the ﬂame propagation time decreases by 63.1%, which

Figure 8 presents the combined eﬀects of the methane and
propane fractions on the maximum ﬂame velocity (Vmax). Vmax
increases continuously with an increasing methane fraction γ.
However, a substantial decrease in Vmax can be observed with
an increase in μ. This contradicts previous observations that
propane addition can encourage methane explosions.17,18,22
The LBV of propane is 1.8 times that of biogas at atmospheric
pressure. The heating value of propane is 2.33 times that of
pure methane.16 To ensure a constant fuel heating value
according to eq 3, an increase in the propane fraction is
accompanied by a decrease in the methane fraction. Addition-
ally, the LBV decreases with increasing the propane fraction
(see Figure 4). Therefore, one can see that as the propane
fraction increases, the ﬂame propagation time decreases (see
Figure 7) and the ﬂame speed decreases (see Figure 8). As μ
increases from 0.00 to 0.43, the percentage reductions of Vmax
are 11.3%, 45.9%, 39.6%, 19.1%, 21.4%, and 16.4% for the six
oxygen fractions. The inhibitory eﬀect of the propane fraction
on Vmax ﬁrst increases and then decreases after reaching the
maximum inhibitory eﬀect at θ = 0.25. Therefore, the propane
fraction signiﬁcantly decreases Vmax (especially at θ = 0.25 and
0.29), which reduces the risk of the oxygen-enriched
combustion.
3.3. Explosion Pressure Dynamics. As shown in Figure
1, two pressure transducers were employed to monitor the
explosion pressure. There are no diﬀerences between the
pressure curves recorded by the two pressure transducers other
than the amplitudes. Therefore, only the pressure at the closed
end was analyzed. Figure 9 presents the explosion pressure
over time for various propane fractions μ and oxygen fractions
θ. There are two types of pressure proﬁles: unimodal and
bimodal. The bimodal overpressure trend appears for (a) θ =
0.21, (b) θ = 0.25, and (c) θ = 0.29. The deﬁnitions of Pb, Pmfa,
and Pext follow those presented by Yang et al. (i.e., Pb is the
bursting pressure, Pmfa occurs when the maximum ﬂame area is
achieved, and Pext occurs as a result of an external explosion).47
As shown in Figure 9a, where μ = 0.23, Pb is caused by the
rupture of the PVC ﬁlm at the open end. A large amount of
unburnt gas is released and the volume expansion rate of initial
combustion is much smaller than the rate of the gas escape,
resulting in an instantaneous pressure drop. Zheng et al.38
pointed out that the dynamic failure pressure depends on the
reactivity of mixtures, meaning it depends on the combination
of μ and θ. Next, an increase in pressure is caused by an
increase in the ﬂame area. Finally, a bimodal overpressure
trend can be observed.
In most cases, Pb is lower than Pmfa in the bimodal pressure
trend. Pmfa is equal to the maximum peak pressure Pmax.
However, Pb is greater than Pmfa when μ is equal to 0.26, 0.28,
0.31, and 0.43 in Figure 9a. At this time, Pb is equal to the
maximum peak pressure Pmax. Additionally, μ = 0.26 is the
inﬂection point of Pmfa > Pb in the bimodal pressure trend.
With an increasing θ, the LBV exhibits a substantial increase
(see Figure 4), similar to the reactivity of the mixture. The
volume expansion rate approaches the rate of gas escape during
the initial combustion stage. The rate of pressure drop
decreases and the duration of the pressure drop decreases from
θ = 0.21 in Figure 9a to θ = 0.29 in Figure 9c. Eventually, the
volume expansion rate of initial combustion exceeds the gas
escape rate. The slope of the net volume generation rate is
always positive, resulting in a continuous increase in pressure,
generating a unimodal pressure trend at θ = 0.35, 0.40, and
0.50.
A third pressure transient Pext can be observed in the later
stages of the explosion overpressure trend, as shown in Figure
9a. This diﬀers from the damped oscillations highlighted in the
previous studies.38 The time to the local pressure peak Pext is
almost the same as the time at which the ﬂame passes out of
the duct. Ponizy and Veyssiere,48 Ferrara et al.,49 and Di Sarli
et al.50 demonstrated that an external explosion outside a vent
duct results in a sudden increase in pressure. Pext can be
attributed to the appearance of a small-scale external explosion.
The premixed fuel discharged by the explosion in the
elongated duct forms a ﬂammable elongated area at the outlet
of the duct, which diﬀers from the approximately spherical
cloud formed at the outlet of the spherical explosion vessel and
the shorter explosion duct. The intensity of the external
explosion was not high in this study and it only occurred at θ =
0.21. Additionally, it was also observed that the time of Pext
appearance is gradually delayed with increasing propane
fraction, as shown in Figure 9a.
Figure 10 presents the variations in Pmax with the propane
fraction μ and oxygen fraction θ with error bars. Pmax decreases

3.4. Rates of Production (ROP) and Radical Distribu-
tion. To investigate the eﬀects of propane addition and oxygen
enrichment on ﬂame propagation at the elementary reactions
level, ROP analysis was performed. As short-lived free radicals
in the combustion reaction zone, H, OH, and O are direct
participants in elementary reactions, which play an important
role in the combustion process.2,53−56 The primary chain-
propagating reactions for producing and consuming H, OH,
and O radicals in the mixtures are illustrated in Figure S2 of
the Supporting Information (SI). R1 (H + O2 ↔OH + O) is
the primary chain-propagating reaction that produces the OH
and O radicals, but it consumes H radical. R3 (H2 + OH ↔
H2O + H) is the dominant chain-propagating reaction that
produces the H radical, but it consumes the OH radical. R49
(CH3 + O ↔CH2O + H) is the main chain-propagating
reaction that contributes to the reduction of O radicals.
Additionally, as μ increases from 0.00 to 0.43 at θ = 0.21, there
is an inhibition inﬂuence on the ROP of the H, OH, and O
radicals. However, as θ slightly increases from 0.21 to 0.25 at μ
= 0.00, a signiﬁcant promotion eﬀect on the ROP of the H,
OH, and O radicals can be observed in Figure S2 (SI).

4. CONCLUSION
The eﬀects of propane addition and oxygen enrichment on the
ﬂame characteristics of biogas were experimentally studied
with a constant heating value in a half-open duct. The ﬂame
evolution, ﬂame propagation speed, pressure proﬁles, max-
imum pressure peaks, maximum rate of pressure rise, rate of
production, and radical distribution were acquired. The main
results can be summarized as follows.
Oxygen enrichment has a more signiﬁcant inﬂuence on
ﬂame structure evolution compared to propane addition. The
evolution of the ﬂame structure revealed that the tulip
structure takes on two types of patterns at the oxygen fraction
θ = 0.21. As the oxygen fraction θ increases, a salient tulip
ﬂame cannot be observed. When θ = 0.21, as the propane
fraction μ increases from 0.00 to 0.43, there are diﬀerent
evolutionary processes of the tulip ﬂame and the evolution
times of diﬀerent ﬂame stages are extended. However, when θ
> 0.21, there are no obvious changes in the ﬂame structure as μ
increases.
The ﬂame front velocity V versus time can be divided into
three patterns. The addition of a small amount of oxygen can
eﬀectively decrease the ﬂame propagation time and improve
the performance of the mixture. Propane addition signiﬁcantly
decreases Vmax (especially at θ = 0.25 and 0.29) and reduces
the explosion risk of the oxygen-enriched mixtures.
Pressure proﬁles exhibit very diﬀerent behaviors depending
on the combination of propane addition and oxygen
enrichment. However, the LBV presents the combined eﬀect
of the propane fraction and oxygen fraction, which is an
important parameter to predict Pmax, (dP/dt)max, and Vmax
values of the mixtures and estimate the explosion risk.
The rate of propane consumption is greater than the rate of
methane consumption, and the consumption of propane ends
earlier than that of methane. Oxygen consumption plays an
important role in the entire reaction process, leading to the
increase in the concentrations of microscopic free radicals and
the promotion eﬀect on the ROP of free radicals. In contrast,
the addition of propane decreased the molar concentrations of
microscopic free radicals and inhibited the ROP of free
radicals.
In the future, the eﬀect of the equivalence ratio on the ﬂame
characteristics of biogas by propane addition and oxygen
enrichment will be studied, and ﬂame accelerations in larger
ducts are deserved to be studied for practical applications.
